name: Peer Review Summaries
title: Peer Review Summaries
answer: Peer review summaries use an AI tool to condense the comments students receive on their drafts into a few clear themes, after names are removed. This matters because scattered notes are hard to act on, while a short summary of patterns, such as several classmates finding the introduction confusing, gives the writer something concrete to work with. The teacher reviews each summary first, and students still read the original comments.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: Peer review teaches students to read writing critically, but the comments it generates can pile up into something a writer cannot easily use. This idea solves that by having the teacher remove student names and run the collected comments through an AI tool, which condenses them into a few clear themes for each writer. Instead of facing a heap of scattered notes, the writer learns that, for example, three classmates found the introduction confusing and two wanted more evidence. The summary turns a mass of individual reactions into a pattern the writer can act on. It keeps the substance of what classmates said while making it usable.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, students first review each other's drafts as they normally would, and the teacher then strips the names from the comments and uses an AI tool to summarize what each writer received into a few themes. The teacher reads every summary before it reaches the student, checking that it stays faithful to what classmates actually said and adding a note of their own where needed. The text describes this practice for reading and writing across kindergarten through twelfth grade rather than assigning it to particular grade bands. Students then read the original comments alongside the summary, so the summary works as a guide into the feedback rather than a replacement for it. The writer ends up with both the pattern and the individual voices behind it.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or formal finding for peer review summaries, so this idea rests on practice rather than research. Its support comes from the described classroom routine and the reasoning that a short set of themes is easier to act on than scattered notes. The text also notes the practical caution that AI tools can soften criticism too much, exaggerate minor points, or miss a comment that matters, which is why the teacher reads the summary first. No evidence label is attached to the idea in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher must review the summaries before students see them, because an AI tool can soften criticism too much, exaggerate minor points, or overlook a comment that matters. That quick read keeps the summary faithful to what classmates actually said and gives the teacher a chance to add a note of their own. The summary is a guide and not a substitute for the conversation between writers, so students should still read the original comments. Some of the most useful feedback is a single sharp comment that no summary will capture, and the human voices of classmates should stay in view. The decisions about what the summary says and what students finally receive stay with the teacher.
